newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Fed focusing on core CPI - NY Fed's Peach.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Fed focusing on core CPI - NY Fed's Peach.

text.p: Economists at the Federal Reserve have moved their focus away from the overall Consumer Price Index (CPI) as the service sector captured a greater share of the U.S. economy in the 1990s, a senior economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York said.
"Economists at the Federal Reserve don't pay too much attention to the total CPI," New York Fed assistant vice president Richard Peach told Reuters in an interview.
But the economist said the core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, has risen in prominence among policy makers.
Peach spoke to Reuters after addressing a conference at the Rockefeller Institute of Government on Thursday.
"The basic research began in 1990 on how we would model inflation," Peach said, noting that "prior to that period, commodities were useful to the CPI."
"As services have increased their weight in their percentage of the economy, commodities prices have dwindled in importance in explaining the aggregate inflation rate," Peach added.
Peach said the 1990s shift toward an increasingly service-oriented U.S. economy has reduced the importance of the CPI as a gauge of inflation.

Peach told the Rockefeller Institute of Government that March-to-May data indicated "the rate of increases of prices of core services may be turning upward ... for the first time in this business cycle."
Data showed the service sector component of the core CPI has been edging higher from a 3.0-percent low earlier this year while the goods component is hovering around 1.0 percent.

Peach, who declined to comment on the Fed's current monetary policy stance, also said that low food and energy prices were key factors contributing to the tame performance of the CPI in the second quarter.

Turning to the inflation-adjusted real federal funds rate, Peach said it was roughly at the same level as in early 1995, at the end of a brisk, year-long tightening cycle that doubled its nominal rate.
However, the current real funds rate does not seem to have the effect of slowing the economy as it did in 1995.

"After slowing to below potential in 1995 in response to a tightening of monetary policy in 1994, growth accelerated in 1996, reaching 4.0 percent, year-over-year, in the first quarter of 1997," Peach said.
The New York Fed senior economist said that a "fundamental question for monetary policy stance today is that (the role of) the real funds rate is not definitely established."
Peach said other parameters put the real funds rate in a different context than in 1994-95.

"I guess one answer to that, and it has been a great deal of research at the New York Fed, is that the credit channels are different," Peach said, adding that financing from car loans to mortgages are currently readily available at competitively low rates and to sub-par borrowers.
Other factors affecting the monetary stance in relation to growth and inflation is that new software programs have allowed "a better management of inventories ... and less volatility in GDP swings."
Also, the Treasury market "is more forward-looking in terms of monetary policy and sort of helping to regulate" the business cycle, Peach noted.

Unlike during the 1994 Fed tightening cycle when a credit market selloff worsened the impact of the Fed's rates hikes, Treasuries this time rallied, helping support the housing and durable goods sectors.
